source_refs.note: Topic 9.5 with Fig. 9.16, Examples 9.4 and 9.5 and the ECG/EEG boxes (PDF 202-204, printed 199-201).

blocks.text: Figure 9.16 shows two oppositely charged parallel plates which produce a uniform electric field. A positive charge q allowed to move in this field will move from plate B to plate A and gain kinetic energy. If it is to be moved from A to B, an external force is needed to move the charge against the electric field, and it will gain potential energy. Let us impose the condition that, as the charge is moved from A to B, it is kept in electrostatic equilibrium, that is, it moves with uniform velocity; this is achieved by applying a force F equal and opposite to qE at every point along its path. The work done by the external force against the field increases the electrical potential energy of the charge.

blocks.alt: A positive charge +q sits between a positive top plate and a negative bottom plate a distance d apart. The field pushes it down with force qE; an equal force F = qE pushes it up against the field. A note says the work done is qE d, so the potential difference is V = E d.
blocks.caption: A charge between oppositely charged plates (original diagram after Figure 9.16).

blocks.text: Let W_AB be the work done by the force in carrying the positive charge q from A to B while keeping it in equilibrium. The change in its potential energy is delta U = W_AB, or U_B - U_A = W_AB ... (9.16), where U_A and U_B are the potential energies at A and B.

blocks.title: Electric potential difference
blocks.text: The potential difference between two points A and B in an electric field is the work done in carrying a unit positive charge from A to B while keeping the charge in equilibrium: delta V = V_B - V_A = W_AB/q = delta U/q ... (9.17), where V_A and V_B are the electric potentials at A and B.

The electric potential energy difference and the electric potential difference are related by delta U = q delta V ... (9.18). Thus the potential difference between two points can be defined as the difference of the potential energy per unit charge. As the unit of potential energy is the joule, Eq. 9.17 shows that the unit of potential difference is the joule per coulomb, called the volt: 1 volt = 1 joule/1 coulomb ... (9.19). That is, a potential difference of 1 volt exists between two points if the work done in moving a 1 coulomb positive charge from one point to the other, keeping equilibrium, is one joule.

To give a concept of electric potential at a point, we need a reference point to which we assign zero electric potential; it is usually taken at infinity. Thus, in Eq. 9.17, if we take point A at infinity and choose V_A = 0, the electric potential at B is V_B = W_AB/q. Generally V = W/q ... (9.20), which states that the electric potential at any point in an electric field is equal to the work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point, keeping it in equilibrium. The potential at a point is therefore always relative to the potential at infinity. Both potential and potential difference are scalar quantities, because both W and q are scalars.

Consider again Fig. 9.16: the field between the plates is uniform, of value E. The potential difference between A and B is V_B - V_A = W_AB/q ... (9.21), where W_AB = Fd = -qEd (the negative sign is needed because F must be applied opposite to qE to keep the charge in equilibrium). So V_B - V_A = -qEd/q = -Ed, or E = -(V_B - V_A)/d = -delta V/d ... (9.22). If the plates are separated by an infinitesimally small distance delta d, E = -delta V/delta d ... (9.23).

The quantity delta V/delta d gives the maximum value of the rate of change of potential with distance, because the charge has been moved along a field line, in which direction the distance delta d between the two plates is minimum; it is known as the potential gradient. Thus the electric intensity is equal to the negative of the gradient of potential; the negative sign indicates that the direction of E is along decreasing potential. From Eq. 9.23 the unit of electric intensity is the volt per metre (V m^-1), which equals N C^-1: 1 V m^-1 = 1 (J C^-1) m^-1 = 1 N m/(m C) = 1 N C^-1.

blocks.title: Example 9.4
blocks.text: Two parallel metal plates 1.0 cm apart are connected to a 12 V battery. Find the electric field intensity between them. Solution: delta V = 12 V, delta d = 1.0 cm = 1 x 10^-2 m. E = delta V/delta d = 12 V/(1 x 10^-2 m) = 1200 V m^-1 (or N C^-1).

blocks.title: Example 9.5
blocks.text: Two horizontal parallel metal plates are connected to a 12 V battery. An electron is released from the negative plate; find its speed as it reaches the positive plate (m = 9.1 x 10^-31 kg, e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C). Solution: the electron is repelled by the negative plate and attracted by the positive plate; the potential energy it loses becomes kinetic energy: delta V x e = (1/2) m v^2, 12 V x 1.6 x 10^-19 C = (1/2) x 9.1 x 10^-31 kg x v^2, so v^2 = 4.2 x 10^12 m^2 s^-2 and v = 2.1 x 10^6 m s^-1.

An ECG records the 'voltage' between points on human skin generated by electrical processes in the heart; an ECG made while running gives information about the heart's performance under stress. In electroencephalography the potential differences created by the electrical activity of the brain are used for diagnosing abnormal behaviour (Do You Know).

blocks.prompt: Explain electric potential and prove that electric field intensity is equal to the negative of the potential gradient (comprehensive question 9.1). Find the potential 50 cm from a 50 uC charge (MCQ 9.5). Why should we wear rubber-soled shoes while handling electric appliances (Point to ponder)?
blocks.explanation: Potential at a point is the work per unit charge in bringing a positive charge from infinity, V = W/q; between plates W_AB = -qEd, so V_B - V_A = -Ed and E = -delta V/delta d, the negative of the potential gradient. V = kq/r = 9 x 10^9 x 50 x 10^-6/0.5 = 9 x 10^5 V, option (c). Rubber is an insulator: it keeps the body from completing a path to earth, so if a live wire is touched little or no current flows through the body.

items: Moving charge q from A to B against E at uniform velocity: delta U = W_AB (9.16). Potential difference delta V = W_AB/q = delta U/q (9.17); delta U = q delta V (9.18); 1 V = 1 J C^-1 (9.19); potential V = W/q from infinity (9.20); scalars.
E = -delta V/delta d (9.23): field equals the negative potential gradient, pointing towards lower potential; V m^-1 = N C^-1. Examples: 1200 V m^-1; 2.1 x 10^6 m s^-1.
